solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Pacific territory’s current feeding Hants resort’s lights? (5,3,7)

annotation.definitionNote: the territory is taken as a whole region, while the answer names its many islands

indicators.note: to feed something is to put food into it, so I goes inside the resort's letters

blocks.note: Southsea is a seaside resort in Hampshire (Hants); the 's adds S; split after SOUTHSEA
I is the symbol for electric current
a bird that lights on a branch lands on it

annotation.surface: An electric current powering the illuminations of a south-coast English resort, as if it were a Pacific colony.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lights' reads as illuminations, a noun, but it is the verb meaning comes down to rest. Hants is the short form of Hampshire, the English county.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by broad category: the islands scattered across the South Pacific make up a territory in the loose geographical sense.

entries.clue: A lot of effort, keeping a couple of Poles in port (7)

indicators.note: a lot of something is most but not all of it, so the last letter goes
to keep something is to hold it, so SWEA holds A and NS
a couple means two, so two of the poles are taken

blocks.note: SWEAT = effort, less its last letter; split around ANS
used as printed
N and S are the North and South poles

annotation.surface: Hard labour carried on by two Polish workers in a harbour town.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Poles' looks like people from Poland; it means the two ends of the earth's axis, North and South.
annotation.definitionFit: Swansea is a port city on the south coast of Wales.

entries.clue: Improper but not outstanding? (5)

blocks.note: UN- is the prefix meaning not
a debt still outstanding is due

annotation.surface: A remark that something is improper even though it is not especially remarkable.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' reads as excellent, but here it means unpaid; the question mark flags the pun on 'not due'.
annotation.definitionFit: Undue means excessive or unwarranted, as in undue influence: improper.

entries.clue: Clownlike character in doctors’ street mostly, one of several (9)

indicators.note: mostly means nearly all, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: HARLEY Street in London is famous for private doctors; less its last letter
a quin is one of quintuplets, five babies born together

annotation.surface: A clown turning up among the medical consulting rooms of a London street.
annotation.walkthrough: Harley Street is the London street lined with private medical practices.
annotation.definitionFit: Harlequin is the masked, diamond-suited comic servant of pantomime and commedia dell'arte.

entries.clue: Genuine German playwright, not British (4)

indicators.note: not says the named thing is absent, so BR is removed

blocks.note: Bertolt Brecht, German dramatist
BR = British, removed from the front

annotation.surface: A claim that a German dramatist is the real thing, and no Brit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Genuine German' looks like one phrase describing the playwright, but only 'Genuine' is the definition; ECHT is itself German for genuine.
annotation.definitionFit: Echt, borrowed from German, means authentic or genuine in English too.

entries.clue: Collaborating investigators changed role in case of protest (8)

indicators.note: changed means altered, so the letters are rearranged
a case is the outside of something, so only the outer letters of protest are used

blocks.note: anagram fodder
outer letters of PROTEST, added to the fodder

annotation.surface: Detectives working together who changed their part during a demonstration.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Role in' reads as part of the story, but those six letters join P and T to be shuffled; 'in' is fodder, not a container word.
annotation.definitionFit: Interpol is the international police organisation through which national forces cooperate.

entries.clue: Fruit supplied by half of them in half of capital (5)

indicators.note: half takes half the letters of the word that follows
in places one piece inside another

blocks.note: first half of LONDON; split after L
second half of THEM

annotation.surface: Fruit provided by half of some group, located in half of a city.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Capital' is the capital city, London; half of each word is used.
annotation.definitionFit: A lemon is the sour yellow citrus fruit.

entries.clue: Beautiful youth thus managed to go north over South America (9)

indicators.note: in a down clue, going north means reading upwards, so the letters run backwards
over means above, and in a down clue the first piece sits on top of the rest

blocks.note: sic is Latin for thus
ran = managed, as a business
S = South
US = the United States

annotation.surface: A handsome young man who managed to travel north across South America.
annotation.walkthrough: 'South America' looks like one place, SA, but it splits into S and US.
annotation.definitionFit: Narcissus is the beautiful youth of Greek myth who fell in love with his own reflection.

entries.clue: Record concealed underneath extremely saucy little spirit (7)

indicators.note: underneath means below, and in a down clue the lower piece comes after
the extremes of a word are its ends, so only its first and last letters are used

blocks.note: outer letters of SAUCY
LP = long-playing record
hid = concealed

annotation.surface: A cheeky little sprite who hid a vinyl record under something naughty.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Concealed' looks like a hidden-word indicator, but it is simply HID.
annotation.definitionFit: A sylphid is a small or young sylph, an airy spirit of folklore.

entries.clue: Photo taken beside tree in army training area (9)

indicators.note: placed next to, so the two pieces sit side by side

blocks.note: the alder is a tree
a shot is a photograph

annotation.surface: A snapshot taken next to a tree on a military training ground.
annotation.walkthrough: Aldershot is a Hampshire town long known as the home of the British Army.
annotation.definitionFit: Aldershot is the garrison town where the British Army has trained since the 1850s.

entries.clue: Lesson from gangster’s girl endlessly sheltering gunmen (5)

indicators.note: without its end, so the last letter is dropped
to shelter someone is to keep them inside, so MOL holds RA

blocks.note: a moll is a gangster's girlfriend; MOLL less its last letter; split around RA
RA = Royal Artillery, the army's gunners

annotation.surface: A lesson learnt from a mobster's girlfriend who hides armed men.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gunmen' suggests hoodlums to match the gangster, but it means artillery soldiers, the Royal Artillery.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: what a fable ends by spelling out is the lesson the reader is meant to take away.

entries.clue: Foreign currency quiet king invested in fish (6)

indicators.note: to invest is also to clothe or surround, so K goes inside EEL

blocks.note: sh! is a call for quiet
an eel is a fish; split around K
K = king in chess

annotation.surface: A monarch quietly investing foreign money in the fishing trade.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Invested' plays on putting money into something, which fits the currency; here it means placed inside.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: Israel's money, foreign to the British solvers the Times writes for.

entries.clue: Fairly outspoken, seemingly like some old Germanic people (8)

blocks.note: frank = outspoken
the suffix -ish means fairly, as in 'tallish'

annotation.surface: Someone rather blunt who seems to resemble an ancient Germanic tribe.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Seemingly' admits the joke: the word looks as if it means rather frank, though it really comes from the tribe's name.
annotation.definitionFit: Frankish means of the Franks, the Germanic people who conquered Gaul and gave France its name.

entries.clue: Enthusiasm that’s more difficult for Cockneys, they say (6)

indicators.note: Cockneys, working-class Londoners, traditionally drop the H at the start of words
what people say is heard, so the answer is spelt from the sound

blocks.note: HARDER = more difficult, with the H dropped

annotation.surface: A remark that keenness comes harder to East Enders.
annotation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic accent 'arder and ardour sound the same.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean burning eagerness, the word coming from Latin ardere, to burn.

entries.clue: Wild ruffian’s frantic speed carved up road (9)

indicators.note: frantic means wildly agitated, so the letters are thrown about
carved up means cut and redistributed, so these letters are rearranged too

blocks.note: anagram fodder
anagram fodder

annotation.surface: A lawless thug speeding madly, cutting other drivers up on the road.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Carved up' reads as the driving slang for cutting in front of someone; here it signals rearrangement.
annotation.definitionFit: A desperado is a reckless outlaw, the wild ruffian of Westerns.

entries.clue: Bewildered politician Fabians initially took advantage of (8)

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the first letter is used

blocks.note: CON = Conservative
first letter of FABIANS
used = took advantage of

annotation.surface: A baffled politician exploited by the Fabian Society.
annotation.walkthrough: The Fabians are a British socialist society, which suits the political picture; only their initial counts.
annotation.definitionFit: Confused and bewildered both mean unable to think clearly.

entries.clue: Classify sailors in Cornish river like brothers (9)

indicators.note: in places RATE and RN inside FAL

blocks.note: the Fal is a river in Cornwall, the county at England's south-west tip; split around RATERN
to rate is to grade or classify
RN = Royal Navy

annotation.surface: Grading sailors on a Cornish river by how brotherly they are.
annotation.walkthrough: The river is not the definition but the outer shell of the answer; 'like brothers' at the end is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Fraternal means brotherly, from Latin frater, brother.

entries.clue: Provide too few pieces for such deliveries? (8)

annotation.definitionNote: the second definition describes the deliveries, so the answer is used as an adjective there

blocks.note: pieces is slang for guns, so this means to supply too few weapons
a bowling action with the hand kept below the shoulder

annotation.surface: Short-changing someone on parts for a batch of deliveries.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pieces' is slang for guns, so to underarm is to supply too few weapons; underarm deliveries are balls bowled with the hand below the shoulder, as in cricket or softball.
annotation.definitionFit: Read as under-arm it means to arm insufficiently; as one word it describes a bowling action below shoulder height.

entries.clue: Tirade about flipping hooter booming (8)

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so the letters run backwards
about means around, so RANT goes around the reversed word

blocks.note: a rant is a tirade; split around ESON
hooter is British slang for nose

annotation.surface: A loud rant about a blasted car horn.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British swear word before 'hooter', which suggests a car horn; the hooter is a nose.
annotation.definitionFit: Resonant means deep and echoing, like a booming voice.

entries.clue: Grew fashionable fruit (7)

blocks.note: rose = grew, went up
hip = fashionable

annotation.surface: A fruit that has grown trendy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Grew' pairs naturally with fruit as growing, but it gives ROSE in the sense of increased.
annotation.definitionFit: A rosehip is the red fruit of the rose, used for syrup and tea.

entries.clue: Local’s account for sweet white wine (6)

blocks.note: a local is a neighbourhood pub, so a bar; the 's adds S
AC = account

annotation.surface: A pub's bill for a bottle of dessert wine.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain 'the local' is the pub nearest home; here it gives BAR, with the apostrophe S kept.
annotation.definitionFit: Barsac is a sweet white wine from the Bordeaux region, much like Sauternes.

entries.clue: Continental port contributing to décor in Thessaloniki (7)

indicators.note: the answer supplies part of the words that follow, so it sits inside them

blocks.note: deCOR IN THessaloniki

annotation.surface: A European port town adding to the interior design of Thessaloniki.
annotation.walkthrough: Thessaloniki is itself a Greek port, drawing the eye; the answer is another Greek port concealed across three words.
annotation.definitionFit: Corinth is a Greek port on the isthmus between the mainland and the Peloponnese.

entries.clue: Like many churches, soaked when lake gets in (8)

indicators.note: L enters the other word, so it goes inside

blocks.note: steeped = soaked; split around L
L = lake, as on maps

annotation.surface: Churches drenched when a lake floods into them.
annotation.walkthrough: The flood picture points to water; STEEPED already means soaked and just takes an L.
annotation.definitionFit: Steepled means having a steeple, a tall spire, as many churches do.

entries.clue: Half-wild canine’s function in Tamworth, perhaps? (2-3)

indicators.note: in means located within, so the function takes place inside the pig

blocks.note: the Tamworth is a breed of pig; perhaps marks it as an example; split around DO
a do is a party or social function

annotation.surface: A feral dog attending an event in the English town of Tamworth.
annotation.walkthrough: Tamworth reads as the Staffordshire town, but it is the ginger pig breed named after it; 'do' is British for a party.
annotation.definitionFit: A pi-dog, or pye-dog, is a half-wild stray dog of Asian villages.

entries.clue: Note by Irishwoman failing to finish biographical sketch (6)

indicators.note: by means next to, so the two pieces sit side by side
not reaching the end, so the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: ME is a variant spelling of MI, the third note of the sol-fa scale
Moira is an Irish girl's name; less its last letter

annotation.surface: A short note from an Irishwoman who never completes her life story.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Note' wants to be MEMO, which leaves IR with no source; the note is ME, and Moira supplies the rest.
annotation.definitionFit: A memoir is a written account of someone's life or memories.

entries.clue: Lyric poem about ancient entertainment venue (5)

blocks.note: an ode is a lyric poem
on = about, concerning

annotation.surface: A poem written about an old theatre.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a container or reversal signal, but it simply gives ON; the word Odeon is also a British cinema chain.
annotation.definitionFit: An odeon was a roofed building in ancient Greece or Rome for musical performances.

entries.clue: Family beginning to languish in jail (4)

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter
in means located within, so the languishing letter sits inside the jail like a prisoner

blocks.note: the can is slang for prison; split around L
first letter of LANGUISH

annotation.surface: A family member starting to waste away in prison.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Languish in jail' is a stock phrase; only its first letter goes into the slang word for prison.
annotation.definitionFit: A clan is an extended family, especially in Scotland.

entries.clue: Vast number briefly concealing a cache (5)

indicators.note: cut short, so the last letter is dropped
to conceal is to hide inside, so HORD holds A

blocks.note: a horde is a vast number; HORDE less its last letter; split around A
used as printed

annotation.surface: A huge crowd briefly hiding a secret stash.
annotation.walkthrough: HOARD and HORDE sound alike, which makes the construction neat.
annotation.definitionFit: A hoard is a hidden store of valuables: a cache.

entries.clue: Talent exercised in articles relating to a legendary continent (9)

indicators.note: exercised means put through its paces, so the letters are moved around
in places the rearranged letters inside the articles

blocks.note: A and AN are the indefinite articles; split around the anagram
anagram fodder

annotation.surface: Talent being shown off in newspaper articles about a legendary lost land.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Articles' suggests newspaper pieces; it means the grammatical articles A and AN.
annotation.definitionFit: Atlantean means of Atlantis, the mythical continent said to have sunk beneath the sea.

entries.clue: Snack meal for one who needs a share? (10,5)

annotation.definition2: meal for one who needs a share?

blocks.note: the British pub snack of bread, cheese and pickle

blocks.clueFragment: meal for one who needs a share?
blocks.note: a ploughshare is a plough's blade, so its user is a ploughman, and this is his midday meal

annotation.surface: A light meal for someone who wants to split it.
annotation.walkthrough: A share is a ploughshare, the blade of a plough, so the one who needs it is a ploughman; the question mark flags the pun.
annotation.definitionFit: A ploughman's lunch is a British pub snack of bread, cheese and pickle.
